key_terms.meaning: A network trained to copy its input to its output through a narrow hidden layer, so the hidden layer must keep only the useful structure of the data.
The narrow layer between encoder and decoder; its width fixes how many numbers describe each input.
The penalty for the output not matching the input, usually mean squared error for real-valued data and cross-entropy for binary or pixel data: L = (1/n)Σ‖xᵢ − x̂ᵢ‖².
An autoencoder fed a corrupted copy of x but asked to reconstruct the clean x, which forces the code to keep real structure and drop noise.
An unobserved variable z that is assumed to generate the observed data x; the model is written p(x, z) = p(z)p(x|z).
The probability of the observed data after hiding z: p(x) = ∫ p(x|z)p(z) dz, a sum or integral over all values of z.
Choosing parameters θ to maximise Σᵢ log pθ(xᵢ), the total log-probability of the training data.
A lower bound on log p(x): ELBO = E_q[log p(x|z)] − KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z)), where q is any distribution over z.
A non-negative measure of how much one distribution differs from another: KL(q‖p) = E_q[log(q(x)/p(x))], equal to zero only when q = p.
Writing a sample z ~ N(μ, σ²) as z = μ + σ·ε with ε ~ N(0, 1), so gradients can flow through μ and σ.
A generator G and a discriminator D trained together: D learns to tell real from fake, G learns to fool D.
min_G max_D E_x[log D(x)] + E_z[log(1 − D(G(z)))], where x is real data and z is a random noise vector.
The generator maps many different z values to the same few outputs, so samples lack variety.
A density factorised by the chain rule as p(x) = Πᵢ p(xᵢ | x₁, …, xᵢ₋₁), one variable at a time.
An autoregressive image model that visits pixels in raster order (row by row) and predicts each pixel from the ones already generated, using a recurrent net.
A density model built from an invertible transform x = f(z); the change-of-variables formula gives the exact log-density.
Sampling from p(x_missing | x_known) instead of p(x), which is how generative models edit, fill and upscale images.
Filling a masked region of an image by sampling values that agree with the observed pixels around it.
Producing a high-resolution image from a low-resolution one, keeping the input's content while adding plausible detail.
Synthetic photo, audio or video made to look like a real person, often with a GAN or a diffusion model.

takeaways: An autoencoder learns a compressed code by being forced to rebuild its own input, and the same encoder–decoder shell later becomes a generative model.
Generative modelling means learning a probability distribution over data; anything hidden that explains the data is a latent variable and must be summed or integrated out.
The VAEs objective is a lower bound on log-likelihood, and it is tractable because the expectation is taken over a cheap approximate posterior rather than the true one.
A GAN replaces an explicit likelihood with a learned test: the discriminator, which is why samples look sharp but training is unstable.
Autoregressive models and normalising flows give exact likelihoods, the first by ordering the variables and the second by stacking invertible transforms.
Editing, inpainting and super-resolution are all the same trick: condition the model on the part of the image you already know.
Generative models inherit the biases of their training data and can be used to make convincing fake media, so evaluation and mitigation are part of the design, not an afterthought.
The choice of model family is a trade-off: exact likelihood versus sharp samples versus stable training versus a usable latent space.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a formula with an explanation of each symbol, a named architecture, and the vision applications (editing, inpainting, super-resolution) with the ethical risks of generative AI.

bank.q: Explain the encoder–decoder structure of an autoencoder. Draw the block diagram, name each part, and state what the bottleneck layer does to the data.
outline: Encoder maps input x to code h = f(x); decoder maps h back to x̂ = g(h).
Training minimises reconstruction loss such as mean squared error or binary cross-entropy over pixels.
The bottleneck is narrower than the input, so the network cannot copy; it must keep the main factors of variation.
A linear autoencoder with squared error spans the same subspace as PCA.
If the bottleneck is wider than the input, the network can learn the identity and becomes useless — this motivates denoising, sparse and variational variants.

bank.q: Define a latent variable model. Write the marginal likelihood for continuous z and explain every term.
outline: z is unobserved, x is observed; joint is p(x, z) = p(z)p(x|z).
p(x) = ∫ p(x|z)p(z) dz for continuous z, and p(x) = Σ_z p(x|z)p(z) for discrete z.
p(z) is the prior over causes; p(x|z) is the likelihood or decoder.
The integral has no closed form for a neural decoder, so exact maximum likelihood is hard.
Maximum likelihood picks θ maximising Σᵢ log pθ(xᵢ).

bank.q: State the GAN minimax objective and explain the role of the generator and the discriminator in the two-player game.
outline: Objective: min_G max_D E_{x~data}[log D(x)] + E_{z~p(z)}[log(1 − D(G(z)))] with D(x) a probability.
Discriminator maximises the objective: it wants D(x) near 1 for real and near 0 for fake.
Generator minimises it: it wants D(G(z)) near 1, i.e. fakes judged real.
At the optimum, for a fixed G the best D is p_data(x)/(p_data(x) + p_g(x)), and the game drives p_g towards p_data.
Training alternates: k steps of D, one step of G, using gradients through D into G.

bank.q: Describe the chain-rule factorisation used by autoregressive image models such as PixelRNN, and explain why the pixel ordering matters.
outline: p(x) = Πᵢ p(xᵢ | x₁, …, xᵢ₋₁) by the chain rule; no approximation is made.
Pixels are ordered in raster scan: top-left to bottom-right, row by row.
Each conditional is a neural net (recurrent for PixelRNN, masked convolution for PixelCNN) with a softmax over 256 intensity values per channel.
The order fixes the conditioning set; a different order gives a different (still valid) factorisation.
Likelihood is exact and training is plain cross-entropy, but sampling is sequential and slow, and no simple low-dimensional latent code exists.

bank.q: What is a normalising flow? Give the change-of-variables formula and state the requirements on the transform.
outline: x = f(z) with z ~ p_z(z), f invertible, z = f⁻¹(x).
log p_x(x) = log p_z(f⁻¹(x)) + log |det ∂f⁻¹/∂x|.
The Jacobian determinant must be cheap to compute, which is why coupling layers with triangular Jacobians are used.
f must be invertible and both f and f⁻¹ must be differentiable.
Stacking flows gives an exact likelihood, unlike VAEs, and gives both sampling and inference in one model.

bank.q: Starting from log p(x), derive the evidence lower bound used to train a VAE, showing every step.
outline: Write log p(x) = log ∫ p(x|z)p(z) dz.
Introduce any distribution q(z|x) and multiply and divide inside the integral.
Use Jensen's inequality (or the KL decomposition) to get log p(x) ≥ E_q[log p(x|z)] + E_q[log p(z) − log q(z|x)].
Identify the second bracket as −KL(q(z|x)‖p(z)).
Final form: ELBO = E_q[log p(x|z)] − KL(q(z|x)‖p(z)), with gap equal to KL(q(z|x)‖p(z|x)).
Reconstruction term trains the decoder; KL term pulls the encoder output towards the prior.

bank.q: For a Gaussian encoder q(z|x) = N(μ, σ²) and a standard normal prior p(z) = N(0, 1), write the closed-form KL term and explain how the sampling step is made differentiable.
outline: For one dimension: KL = ½(σ² + μ² − 1 − log σ²), summed over latent dimensions.
It is zero when μ = 0 and σ² = 1, i.e. the encoder output matches the prior.
Reparameterisation: sample ε ~ N(0,1), set z = μ + σ ⊙ ε.
Gradients now flow through μ and σ, so backpropagation works through a random node.
The encoder outputs log σ² rather than σ² for numerical stability.

bank.q: A VAE is trained on face images. Explain how you would edit an image by moving in the latent space, and what you must check before trusting the result.
outline: Encode the image: z = μ(x), or sample z ~ q(z|x).
Find a direction d for the attribute (smile, age) by averaging latent differences between labelled pairs.
Decode z + αd for increasing α and watch the attribute change while identity stays fixed.
Large α leaves the region covered by the prior and produces unrealistic images, because the decoder was never trained there.
Check disentanglement: one attribute should change, others should stay; otherwise the direction is entangled.
Report both the reconstruction and the KL term; a collapsed posterior gives weak edits.

bank.q: Describe how to inpaint a missing region of an image using a pretrained generative model, and how the mask changes the objective.
outline: Split the image into known pixels x_k and missing pixels x_m with mask M.
Sample from the conditional p(x_m | x_k), not the unconditional p(x).
With a VAE, optimise the latent code so the decoded known region matches x_k, then fill x_m from the same decode.
With a GAN, train or use a conditional GAN whose loss is weighted by the mask, plus a context loss on known pixels.
Fill must be consistent at the boundary; check for blur and for multiple plausible completions.

bank.q: Design a super-resolution pipeline for old scanned photographs using a generative model. State the losses and the evaluation you would use.
outline: Downsample high-resolution images to make paired low/high training data, or use unpaired data with a CycleGAN-style setup.
Generator: an encoder–decoder or residual CNN that upsamples by the scale factor.
Pixel loss (L1 or L2) keeps colours and structure; adversarial loss adds sharp texture; perceptual loss on pretrained features keeps identity.
Mean squared error alone gives blurry output because it averages over plausible high-frequency details.
Evaluate with PSNR and SSIM for fidelity plus a human or feature-based check for realism.
State the failure mode: the model may hallucinate detail that was never in the original, which matters for forensic or medical use.

bank.q: Compare VAEs and GANs on likelihood, sample sharpness, training stability and usefulness of the latent space.
outline: VAE maximises a lower bound on likelihood; GANs give no explicit likelihood and only an implicit density.
VAE samples are often blurry because the Gaussian decoder and the averaged reconstruction loss smooth detail; GAN samples are sharp.
GAN training is a saddle-point game with no guaranteed convergence and suffers mode collapse; VAE training is a single stable objective.
VAE gives a smooth, continuous latent space that supports interpolation and editing; the GAN latent space is usable but less directly probabilistic.
VAE has the KL term to control the code; a too-strong KL term causes posterior collapse.
Choose VAE for density-based or editing tasks, GAN for photorealism; combination models such as VAE–GAN hybrids and diffusion models try to get both.

bank.q: A GAN produces only a handful of distinct faces from many noise vectors. Diagnose the problem and evaluate three remedies.
outline: Diagnosis: mode collapse — many z map to the same output, and the discriminator's gradient stops pushing towards missing modes.
Remedy 1: minibatch features so D sees the whole batch and penalises low variety.
Remedy 2: Wasserstein loss with weight clipping or gradient penalty, giving smoother gradients everywhere.
Remedy 3: unrolled GAN or experience replay to reduce the game's oscillation.
Also: check the architecture and learning rates, and add a diversity metric (e.g. FID plus a coverage measure) to the evaluation.
Evaluate each remedy on sample variety, not only on visual quality, and state the extra compute cost.

bank.q: Why is exact maximum likelihood easy for autoregressive models and normalising flows but hard for VAEs? Compare the three families on this point.
outline: Autoregressive: the chain rule gives an exact factorisation, and each conditional is a neural softmax; log-likelihood is a direct sum.
Flows: invertible transforms plus the Jacobian determinant give an exact log-density in closed form.
VAE: the integral over z is intractable, so we optimise a lower bound; the gap is KL(q(z|x)‖p(z|x)).
Cost: autoregressive sampling is sequential and slow; flows need invertible, dimension-preserving architectures; VAEs sample fast in one pass but only bound the likelihood.
Implication: comparing log-likelihood numbers across families is not apples to apples for VAEs.

bank.q: A start-up launches a face-editing and voice-cloning app built on a GAN. Evaluate the bias, toxicity and deepfake risks and propose concrete mitigations.
outline: Bias: training data under-represents some groups, so edits and reconstructions fail or distort them; measure error per group, not only overall averages.
Toxicity: the model can be steered to abusive content; filter training data, add input and output classifiers, and provide reporting.
Deepfakes: realistic fake video enables fraud, non-consensual imagery and disinformation; add consent checks, visible or invisible watermarking, and provenance metadata.
Legal and platform context: consent for face and voice data, age limits, takedown process, and logs of model use.
Evaluation is part of the model: red-team before release, publish a model card, monitor after release.
Trade-off: stronger output filters reduce misuse but also block legitimate uses; state the policy explicitly.

glossary.def: A neural network trained to reconstruct its input through a narrow hidden code.
The narrowest layer of an autoencoder, which holds the compressed code.
The space of hidden codes z in which each input becomes a point or a distribution.
The difference between the input and the autoencoder's output, used as the training loss.
An autoencoder whose code is smaller than the input, so it must discard information.
An autoencoder trained to recover clean input from a corrupted version of it.
A model that explains observed data through unobserved variables, p(x, z) = p(z)p(x|z).
The distribution p(z) assumed over the latent variable before seeing any data.
The distribution p(z|x) of the latent variable given the observed data.
The probability of the data after integrating out the latent variable, p(x) = ∫ p(x|z)p(z) dz.
Approximating a hard posterior p(z|x) with a simpler, tractable family q(z|x).
A tractable lower bound on log p(x) used as the VAE training objective.
A non-negative measure of the difference between two probability distributions, zero only when they match.
Rewriting a random sample as a deterministic function of the parameters plus fixed noise, so gradients pass through.
The failure where a VAE's encoder ignores the input and q(z|x) equals the prior, so z carries no information.
The network in a GAN that turns a noise vector into a fake sample.
The network in a GAN that scores how likely a sample is to be real rather than generated.
A GAN failure where the generator produces only a few distinct outputs.
A density model that predicts each variable from the variables before it in a fixed order.
An autoregressive image model that generates pixels one at a time in raster order using a recurrent network.
A density model built from a stack of invertible, differentiable transforms with tractable Jacobian determinants.
Filling in a missing or masked region of an image in a way that agrees with its surroundings.
Generating a high-resolution image from a low-resolution input.
Synthetic media that realistically depicts a person saying or doing something they did not.
